rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the late-elution penalty. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Change temperature alone to probe selectivity in the crowded four-peak cluster and the late doublet. Keeping the gradient fixed makes the temperature response interpretable, with ample room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Halve the gradient slope at the better-performing temperature to test whether the remaining close pairs separate through slope-dependent selectivity. The current short elution window leaves room for a longer gradient without necessarily incurring a time penalty.

Further reduce the gradient slope to improve the sole remaining critical pair, which gained resolution when tG increased to 20 minutes. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving a chance to achieve full resolution without a time penalty.

The late critical pair converged as tG increased from 20 to 24 minutes, so test a slightly steeper gradient than the best run. At 18 minutes, that pair may reach baseline resolution while the earlier cluster retains sufficient separation.

This gives a slope of 0.045 organic fraction/min, just steeper than injection 5’s 0.04444, targeting the late pair’s tiny resolution deficit while preserving the early separations. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated composition at the last peak’s elution.

Injection 6 has reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter elution window. Raising both endpoints by 0.05 preserves the gradient slope while probing whether a stronger starting composition can accelerate elution without sacrificing full resolution.

Slightly flatten the gradient to recover separation in the early cluster lost at the higher starting composition. This tests whether full resolution can be restored while keeping the last peak earlier than in injection 6, which remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a small temperature change to alter selectivity in the two limiting pairs, since flattening the gradient further risks improving one while worsening the other. Injection 6 remains the maximum-score fallback while this explores a potentially faster fully resolved method.

Return to the successful starting composition and test a small slope increase, from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute, to shorten elution. This probes the full-resolution boundary closely while retaining injection 6 as the proven maximum-score method.

Test whether a weaker starting composition can preserve separation in the early cluster while a steeper gradient accelerates the late peaks. Injection 6 remains the proven maximum-score method; this explores a different balance of initial retention and gradient slope.

The high-temperature neighborhood is tightly constrained, with injection 6 already achieving maximum CRF. Test the low-temperature endpoint using the original scouting gradient to look for a different selectivity regime that could support a faster fully resolved method.

Reduce the slope at 25 C to test whether both remaining critical pairs improve in this alternative selectivity regime. The 6.34-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution while staying below the time-penalty threshold.

The middle critical pair converged when the gradient was flattened, so test a steeper gradient to separate it and shorten elution. This also measures whether the late pair remains limiting before adjusting temperature or starting composition.

Raise temperature by one step at the fast low-temperature method to probe selectivity in its three moderately unresolved pairs. Keep injection 6 as the maximum-score benchmark while testing whether this shorter elution window can achieve full resolution.

Test a higher starting composition with a shallower gradient in the low-temperature regime to move beyond the middle-pair crossover seen in injection 13. The stronger start should limit the elution-time increase, while injection 6 remains the proven maximum-score fallback.

Test a substantially shallower gradient to move past the middle-pair co-elution and recover separation on the other side of the crossover. Raising the starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 6 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step now that the middle pair appears to have crossed elution order under the shallower gradient. This may improve its resolution while shortening retention, with all other pairs currently comfortably resolved.
Flatten the gradient at 30 C to improve the sole unresolved pair on this side of the crossover. The current last peak at 7.26 minutes leaves room for the retention increase without a time penalty.

Lower temperature one step to separate the late doublet that became limiting in injection 19. Earlier results suggest the middle-pair resolution changes little between 25 and 30 C, so this may preserve its newly achieved separation while resolving the last pair.

Raise both gradient endpoints by 0.05 while preserving the slope of the fully resolved low-temperature method. This tests whether its elution window can be shortened without losing the middle pair’s modest resolution margin.

Increase the starting organic fraction another step at the same slope to test for renewed middle-pair separation beyond the apparent crossover near phi0 0.30. This could yield a faster fully resolved method; injection 6 remains the proven maximum-score fallback.

Injection 22 is now the fastest fully resolved method, with a minimum resolution of 1.88. Raise both endpoints another 0.05 at unchanged slope to test whether elution can be shortened further while retaining full resolution.

Back off to the fully resolved starting composition from injection 22 and shorten the gradient to accelerate elution. Its resolution margins provide room to test a steeper slope, while avoiding the pair that became limiting at phi0 0.40.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-time step to seek earlier elution while preserving its minimum resolution of 1.82. Injection 24 remains the fastest proven maximum-score fallback if this steeper gradient pushes a pair below 1.5.
